raw_text:
The objective of this research is to investigate and explain the observed persistent completion-time differences between sites employing what appear to be identical nominal work processes. The scope includes identifying measurable factors that contribute to these differences, evaluating competing explanations through the Bayesian framework, and determining observations that would clarify these explanations.

Assumptions
- Completion times are a reliable indicator of process efficiency.
- Work processes appear to be identical when analyzed at a nominal level.
- Variations in completion times are due to difference in measurable factors.
- Bayesian methodology provides a credible framework for evaluating competing explanations.

Research design
This study will utilize a Bayesian approach, where hypotheses about the factors contributing to completion-time differences will be formulated. An exploratory phase will initially identify potential factors based on prior knowledge and observations. Subsequently, a confirmatory phase will test these hypotheses using empirical data, applying Bayesian statistics to update the probabilities of the hypotheses as more evidence becomes available.

Data or evidence needed
The required data include:
- Completion times for each site over a substantial period.
- Information about the observable factors such as resource allocation, employee skills, technology usage, and environmental conditions at the sites.
- Observational data on procedural compliance and any deviations from the nominal process.

Measurement
Completion times will be recorded using accurate time-tracking tools. Observable factors will be measured on a continuity scale, capturing the extent to which they conform to standards or previous performances. Observational data will be recorded through direct inspections and monitoring systems.

Analysis
The analysis will follow a Bayesian approach, starting with prior beliefs about the relevance of each hypothesized factor. As the study progresses, Bayes' theorem will be applied to update these beliefs based on the collected data. This probabilistic approach allows for the integration of new evidence with prior knowledge, facilitating a nuanced evaluation of competing explanations.

Decision / stopping rule
The study will conclude when a consensus is reached among competing explanations, defined as when a particular hypothesis reaches a high degree of probability (e.g., 95%) based on accumulated evidence. The research may also cease if resource limitations make further data collection impractical.

Limitations
- Subject to the accuracy of the collected data, which may introduce measurement errors.
- Possibility of omitted variable bias if unobserved factors significantly influence completion times.
- Requires a substantial dataset to provide reliable Bayesian updates.
- Assumes a stationary relationship between the factors and completion times, which may change over time.
